item.title: The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory
item.description:
The industrialization of AI: 8 critical considerations for building an AI gigafactory

The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has transcended the boundaries of corporate software innovation, sparking a foundational transformation in global infrastructure. Across the globe, nations, research institutions, and large enterprises are shifting away from traditional data center models toward massive, centralized hubs designed explicitly to industrialize AI workloads at an unprecedented scale.

As the European Commission works to establish multiple facilities dedicated to training next-generation AI models with trillions of parameters, a new term has emerged to describe these monumental engineering feats: the AI gigafactory.

While a standard corporate AI setup might utilize a few hundred or thousand GPUs, an AI gigafactory scales up to tens or hundreds of thousands of nodes. Power requirements shift dramatically from standard line-item budgeting to a fundamental physical constraint measured in megawatts or even gigawatts.

For CIOs and technology leaders tasked with planning these multi-million-dollar investments, success requires designing the infrastructure from the ground up to support a decade-long operational lifespan.

Based on an architectural white paper from HPE and AMD, here are the eight critical considerations that technology leaders must address when planning a giga-scale AI facility.

  1. Start with power and land
    At the gigafactory scale, raw electrical power dictates the viability of the entire project. Many organizations discover late in the planning cycle that the existing power grid cannot support their computational roadmap, requiring years of utility redesigns, substation overhauls, and transmission line upgrades. Furthermore, because these facilities represent critical infrastructure for national sovereignty and data security, they require physical placement near both primary power grids and robust, independent backup generation sources.
  2. Design for liquid cooling
    Modern high-performance AI chips generate intense thermal output, and compounding this heat across high-density server racks makes traditional air cooling obsolete. Liquid cooling architectures absorb heat significantly faster and can transport up to 3,000 times more heat than standard air systems while utilizing less energy to operate. However, implementing liquid cooling introduces architectural complexities including leak detection systems, precise water-use management, and strict regulatory and insurance sign-offs that must be integrated early in the design phase.
  3. Overbuild your networking capability
    While compute power scales linearly, the communication network must scale exponentially. Large language models are split across thousands of interconnected nodes, and every training iteration requires synchronized communication. Network bottlenecks cause expensive GPUs to sit idle, wasting millions in operational overhead. To future-proof a giga-scale facility, experts advise over-engineering network bandwidth and latency upfront rather than attempting costly retrofits later.
  4. Plan for hardware and software failure
    In a cluster operating with tens of thousands of compute nodes, hardware components will inevitably fail. Gigafactory resilience requires a shift away from standard troubleshooting toward autonomous, self-healing infrastructures. System architects must design independent fault domains, allowing specific operational units to be swapped out or repaired without disrupting the broader, ongoing training workloads.
  5. Deploy orchestration and governance before hardware
    Orchestration software cannot be treated as an afterthought or bolted on after the physical servers are installed. Technology leaders must deploy governance, scheduling, and resource allocation layers first, as these software frameworks directly influence physical hardware requirements, network segmentation, and systemic security boundaries. Pre-defining these parameters ensures that workloads can begin executing safely the moment the physical infrastructure goes live.
  6. Choose your suppliers wisely
    Building at this extreme scale demands technology partners with verified, proven experience in high-performance computing (HPC). For instance, HPE currently powers some of the world’s fastest supercomputers and offers standardized, engineering-validated AI factories to streamline deployment. Concurrently, selecting hardware built on open ecosystems—such as AMD EPYC™ CPUs, AMD Instinct™ GPUs, and AMD Pensando™ DPUs—mitigates vendor lock-in risk and ensures long-term flexibility, high energy efficiency, and sustained return on investment across decades of operation.
  7. Maximize utilization
    Due to the substantial capital expenditure required to establish an AI gigafactory, maximizing utilization is a financial necessity. Interestingly, giga-scale systems operate more efficiently and reliably under heavy, continuous workloads, as stable utilization allows hardware to fail more predictably and exposes systemic bugs early. Cultivating this environment requires fine-grained job scheduling, multi-tenant isolation, and intelligent queuing built directly into the technology stack.
  8. Establish a comprehensive communications plan
    The final consideration extends beyond technical architecture into public policy and stakeholder communication. Because many large-scale AI hubs leverage public funds or impact localized utility resources, management teams must maintain a proactive public relations strategy. Establishing reporting transparency for fund allocation, sustainability metrics, and milestones—while preparing contingency communication strategies for timeline adjustments—helps build lasting community and institutional support.

Building for the future

An AI gigafactory represents far more than a standard data center expansion; it is a generational investment that acts as a launchpad for economic progress, scientific discovery, and national competitiveness. By addressing these core engineering, architectural, and operational constraints early, technology leaders can ensure their high-performance computing initiatives deliver sustained value, resilience, and operational sovereignty in an increasingly interconnected global economy.

For more information, read 8 Considerations for Building an AI Gigafactory.

item.title: The rise of sovereign AI factories: Why the C-suite is rejecting cloud dependency
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has reached a critical strategic inflection point. For the past several years, the prevailing enterprise narrative dictated that cutting-edge AI belonged naturally in the public cloud. However, new data reveals a massive shift in how the world’s most critical infrastructure sectors are approaching accelerated computing. The era of blind cloud dependency is giving way to a new paradigm: the sovereign AI factory.

According to Intersect360 Research, national sovereign AI data centers have become the fastest-growing segment of accelerated computing infrastructure globally. Spending exploded from $1.6 billion in 2023 to $7.2 billion in 2024—a staggering 349% year-over-year increase that outpaces hyperscale AI and AI-focused cloud providers alike. Looking ahead, this market is projected to reach $122.8 billion by 2026, driven by a 90.4% compound annual growth rate (CAGR).

For C-level executives, this trend is not just about expanding server footprints. It represents a fundamental structural realignment of data sovereignty, national security, and strategic autonomy.

The convergence of HPC and AI

Drawing on market data and insights from the HPC-AI Leadership Organization (HALO) uncovers a crucial architectural truth: sovereign AI installations are fundamentally high-performance computing (HPC) centers operating under intense AI pressure.

Rather than building isolated silos or throwing data into standard cloud instances, organizations are consolidating their infrastructure. Intersect360 Research found that 62.5% of surveyed organizations run their traditional HPC and AI workloads on the exact same systems. Similarly, 67.1% leverage the same shared storage layer for both workloads.

This shared infrastructure model is born out of necessity. Traditional scientific modeling and simulation continue to drive baseline technical requirements, while AI training workloads are layered directly on top of them. This reality favors a technology stack that builds upon proven, highly optimized HPC designs rather than purely cloud-native or enterprise-only architectures.

The strict requirement for on-premises control

For sovereign AI initiatives—such as Japan’s AI Bridging Cloud Infrastructure or the G42 cloud in the UAE—keeping critical workloads off the public cloud is a mandatory constraint. The data confirms that 56.3% of sites keep active HPC-AI compute entirely on-premises, and 68.2% do the same for their storage.

When asked to rate the importance of system features for their next infrastructure purchase, buyers rated cloud integration lowest, scoring it a mere 2.25 out of 5. In fact, 36% of respondents classified cloud integration as “not important at all.”

Because data and workloads cannot be offloaded to external providers due to regulatory, national jurisdiction, and security boundaries, on-premises systems must be engineered for flawless execution without a cloud safety net.

Uncovering the industry’s technical bottlenecks

The true value of the data lies in its “satisfaction gap” analysis, highlighting exactly where current market offerings fail to meet the rigorous demands of sovereign environments.

Sovereign AI buyers are optimizing their configurations around fast data movement, not just raw processing numbers (or peak FLOPS). Buyers placed the highest importance on memory or system bandwidth (scoring 4.57 out of 5) and GPU performance (4.53). However, memory bandwidth also yielded the largest satisfaction gap in the industry at 0.86. If data cannot move to the processors fast enough, training speeds stall, introducing severe strategic bottlenecks.

Similar infrastructure pain points appear across fabrics and storage:

  • Networking and interconnects: Interconnect topology is viewed as highly strategic. While architectures have largely standardized on InfiniBand (76.5% as primary) and high-speed Ethernet (68.1% as secondary) scaling from 100 to 400Gbps, users still report significant industry shortfalls in latency, congestion management, and container orchestration.
  • Storage hurdles: Data storage is viewed as strategically vital by 93% of respondents. Parallel file systems (81.2% importance) and tight data locality (83.5% importance) function as core sovereignty enforcement mechanisms. Yet, the industry’s single largest satisfaction gap sits at a glaring 0.98 for storage performance when handling millions of small files—a hallmark of AI training data sets.

To resolve these gaps, market leaders like HPE, utilizing high-bandwidth AMD CPUs and GPUs, are designing configurable, memory-rich on-premises architectures. These systems are purpose-built to balance both large checkpoint-style HPC files and small AI objects within a unified sovereign boundary.

3 practical tips for the C-suite

As your organization navigates the shift toward localized, high-performance AI deployment, keep these data-driven principles in mind:

  1. Treat storage locality as a security strategy: Do not view storage as a generic commodity. Leverage parallel file systems to maintain strict physical control over your training data and model weights, ensuring they remain firmly under your legal jurisdiction.
  2. Prioritize node bandwidth over raw FLOPS: When evaluating vendor hardware, optimize your system configurations around memory bandwidth and fabric predictability rather than simple processor speeds. Bandwidth is the ultimate governor of real-world AI training performance.
  3. Seek co-design partners, not product vendors: Sovereign AI requires balanced, highly specialized, and supportable architecture. Partner with infrastructure ecosystems—like HPE and AMD—that can co-design flexible compute nodes, high-speed networking, and custom services tailored to mixed HPC-AI environments.

Ready to architect your own sovereign AI strategy? Read the full Intersect360 Research report to explore the complete data set and blueprint for the future of on-premises sovereign AI factories.

item.title: Northern Trust streamlines client onboarding with AI agent
item.description:
Venerable Chicago-based banking institution Northern Trust today unveiled a new AI-powered client onboarding agent to streamline the process of bringing institutional clients onto Northern Trust Asset Servicing’s Front Office Solutions platform.

The agent, which transforms years of data and transaction history into a standardized format ready for use in the bank’s reporting environment, is the result of an expanded collaboration with Microsoft.

Developed jointly by Northern Trust and forward deployed engineering (FDE) teams from Microsoft Frontier Company, the agent has cut data preparation time by 83%, from two-and-a-half weeks to just three days.

“Onboarding a large institutional client can involve an enormous amount of data, particularly in alternative investments,” says Northern Trust COO Pete Cherecwich. “You might have years of transaction history and cash flows across multiple investments, and the data can come to us in all kinds of different formats.”

Northern Trust

Until now, Northern Trust had to map and transform that data manually before loading the data into its environment.

“This seemed like a really good problem for AI because there’s a lot of complexity and variability in the data, but there are also patterns that the technology can learn,” Cherecwich adds. “The agent does a lot of the heavy lifting, and then our people review the output and handle the things where there’s uncertainty. That’s the sweet spot for us: let the technology do what it does well and let our people apply their expertise where it matters.”

Agentic skillset

Cherecwich notes the agent, which consolidates large volumes of investment and transaction data from multiple sources to reconstruct performance histories, achieves over a 96% F1 first-pass quality score, an AI evaluation metric of the correctness and completeness of the mappings it produces.

The agent was also evaluated using only anonymized data to ensure client data was securely governed throughout the process. The partners say this eyes off approach has allowed them to achieve production-scale performance while meeting the stringent data stewardship requirements of the highly regulated financial services industry.

“When I think about ROI, I wouldn’t look at just one number,” Cherecwich says. “It’s speed to revenue, the client experience, and taking a very manual process and making it more efficient. It’s allowing our people to spend less time moving data around and more working with clients.”

From the ground up

The partners built the agent on Microsoft Azure. It uses Microsoft Foundry for enterprise AI and integrates with Microsoft 365 tools like Microsoft Excel and SharePoint. Azure provides a governed intelligence layer to preserve approved onboarding knowledge to support continuous improvement of the onboarding process.

The agent is a result of one of Microsoft Frontier Company’s earliest client engagements. Microsoft launched the $2.5 billion venture in July to provide clients support from FDEs that help them overcome the hurdle of moving from AI trials to deploying frontier AI at scale.

“We felt like we needed to organize ourselves differently to be able to serve customers at the speed and scale they want,” says Bill Borden, CVP at Worldwide Financial Services, Microsoft. “We organized Frontier Company as we’ve been thinking about what makes a company ‘frontier’ and on the outer edge to take advantage of what AI can do.”

Microsoft

Part of that process has been studying Microsoft’s internal AI transformation. Those lessons have led Microsoft Frontier Company to bring together not only hands-on engineering teams, but also industry experts in energy and power, manufacturing, automotive, and government, for instance. Team members with expertise in change management and process optimization are also key parts of the mix.

“We now have a really powerful organization that can sit with customers, understand their business processes and their challenges, and understand how we can actually leverage the tech,” Borden says.

Cherecwich agrees those capabilities are what allowed the collaboration between Northern Trust and Microsoft Frontier Company to bear fruit.

“We know asset servicing, our clients, and what a capital call or a valuation looks like even when the data comes in a strange format,” he says. “Microsoft knows AI and the underlying technology. You really needed both. I don’t think either side could have built as good a solution by themselves. And having Microsoft’s engineers embedded with our people and our expertise allowed us to move a lot faster.”

item.title: The open ecosystem imperative: Why mega-enterprises are trading locked vendors for shared foundations
item.description:
The traditional enterprise IT model—relying entirely on proprietary, single-vendor tech stacks—is fracturing under the weight of hyperscale demands. For extra-large (XL) enterprises, especially those that maintain robust in-house engineering teams and write their own code, true infrastructure control is no longer a luxury. It is a core competitive requirement.

To survive in a cloud-native world, forward-thinking CIOs are shifting their strategy away from vendor lock-in and toward an integrated, open ecosystem. By anchoring their infrastructure on Open Compute Project (OCP) designs, open standards, and open source software, mega-enterprises are reclaiming ownership of their technology destiny and driving unprecedented innovation.

1. Stripping out the proprietary hardware premium

For an enterprise operating at massive scale, the “vendor tax” on proprietary hardware and software scales linearly, creating an unsustainable financial burden. Open Compute Project (OCP) standards redefine this economic equation by shifting control back to the buyer.

By adopting open hardware specifications, XL enterprises can procure highly efficient data center infrastructure.

  • Zero bloat: OCP designs eliminate unnecessary cosmetic plastic, proprietary management chips, and redundant power supplies.
  • Drastic cost reductions: Enterprises operating at scale routinely see capital expenditure cuts on hardware alone.
  • Operational savings: The streamlined, vanity-free design of open hardware translates directly to reduced power consumption and easier physical maintenance. This structural shift allows enterprise teams to focus their capital on software differentiation rather than premium hardware markups.

2. Radical agility for in-house engineering teams

When an XL enterprise boasts a mature, in-house team of software engineers, proprietary platforms become an operational cage. If a development team hits an edge-case bug or needs a custom integration in a closed-source system, they are forced to open a support ticket and wait weeks—or months—for a vendor’s product roadmap to align with their urgent business needs.

Open source software virtually eliminates this friction.

  • Direct access to the source: In-house developers can inspect, debug, and modify the underlying code of their infrastructure software immediately.
  • Accelerated feature velocity: If a critical security patch or a custom API integration is required, internal teams can build, test, and deploy it in hours rather than waiting on a vendor’s life cycle.
  • Attracting elite talent: Top-tier software engineers want to work with open-source technologies (like Kubernetes, Linux, and OpenTelemetry) and contribute back to upstream communities. A rigid, proprietary tech stack acts as a hiring deterrent; an open stack is a talent magnet.

3. Supply chain resiliency through interoperable open standards

Recent years have exposed the vulnerability of relying on single-vendor supply chains. When a proprietary hardware vendor faces component shortages, experiences a sudden degradation in service quality, or shifts its licensing model, it leaves clients exposed.

Open standards can serve as an operational insurance policy.

  • Interoperability by design: When APIs, networking protocols, and data formats conform to rigorous, industry-wide open standards, components become modular and interchangeable.
  • Unprecedented optionality: If Vendor A cannot deliver routing switches or server chassis on time, the enterprise can seamlessly swap in compliant alternatives from Vendor B or C without rewriting a single line of internal application code.
  • Procurement leverage: Knowing that an enterprise can walk away from a vendor without undergoing a multimillion-dollar re-engineering effort completely shifts pricing power back to the CIO during contract renewals.

4. Enterprise-grade scale: Enterprise hardware meets open architecture

Implementing an open framework at an XL enterprise does not mean sacrificing the reliability or support that large-scale operations require. Instead, it means partnering with major infrastructure leaders who actively build for open ecosystems.

A prime example of this hybrid approach is deploying open-standard architectures using HPE ProLiant XD245 servers powered by AMD EPYC™ processors.

  • High-density performance: AMD EPYC™ processors deliver the massive core counts and memory bandwidth required to run complex, in-house applications and containerized microservices at scale.
  • Open security standards: HPE’s Silicon Root of Trust protects firmware down to the silicon level, aligning directly with open-source zero-trust security initiatives.
  • Flexibility without lock-in: By leveraging enterprise-grade platforms like HPE and AMD that fully embrace open specifications, CIOs get the best of both worlds: robust, high-performance physical hardware coupled with the architectural freedom to run their own custom-written software layers seamlessly.

5. Co-innovation and compounding community ecosystems

One of the most overlooked benefits of an open framework for XL enterprises is the ability to leverage a global R&D ecosystem. When an internal engineering team builds on top of open standards, they are not innovating in a vacuum; they are standing with giants.

  • Shared security guardrails: Open-source frameworks undergo continuous, rigorous auditing by thousands of independent developers worldwide, meaning vulnerabilities are often spotted and patched before they can impact production environments.
  • Avoiding reinventing the wheel: Instead of building foundational modules from scratch, in-house developers can leverage robust, community-maintained frameworks and focus 100% of their energy on writing proprietary code that directly impacts the company’s bottom line or unique user experience.
  • Future-proofing architecture: As technology cycles accelerate—particularly around intensive cloud and distributed workloads—open ecosystems evolve natively with industry trends so the enterprise’s underlying fabric doesn’t grow obsolete.

6. Designing a high-velocity, lock-in-free future

For XL enterprises, the ultimate goal of an open ecosystem is architectural autonomy. Writing your own code is only half the battle; that code must run on a foundation that your organization fully controls.

By combining open-source software with open-standard APIs and high-performance Open Compute hardware, enterprises build a unified, highly portable infrastructure fabric. This allows workloads to shift dynamically between private data centers and multiple public clouds based purely on cost, performance, and compliance requirements. By eliminating exit fees and avoiding re-platforming, the business remains agile enough to pivot whenever the market demands it.

The bottom line

For CIOs of XL enterprises, adopting an open philosophy is no longer an ideological choice; it is an operational and financial mandate. By grounding infrastructure in Open Compute, open standards, and open source, organizations unlock the potential of their internal engineering talent. By utilizing high-performance platforms like HPE ProLiant and AMD EPYC, they insulate themselves from supply chain shocks and build a high-velocity digital platform designed for perpetual innovation.

The CIO open infrastructure readiness checklist

Before transitioning your workloads to an open architecture, ensure your organization has audited the following critical operational pillars:

  • Audit vendor dependency: Identify any software dependencies that lock your custom code to proprietary hardware APIs.
  • Evaluate compute density: Benchmark current workloads against high-core-count architectures, such as HPE ProLiant servers powered by AMD EPYC processors, to optimize data center footprint.
  • Assess developer workflows: Verify that internal software engineering teams have direct, friction-free access to debug and patch underlying open-source infrastructure tools.
  • Review procurement modularity: Ensure hardware supply chain strategies include standard-compliant alternatives that can be hot-swapped without software refactoring.
  • Establish upstream guidelines: Implement clear corporate policies for how internal developers contribute bug fixes and feature patches back to open-source communities safely.

item.title: AI agents shouldn’t grade their own work
item.description:
On July 16, Hugging Face disclosed that an autonomous agent system had breached part of its production infrastructure. Five days later, OpenAI identified its own models as responsible. Its subsequent investigation described agents operating under reduced safeguards, exploiting flaws in shared infrastructure, and reaching the internet through a package-management service. They exchanged discoveries on an improvised message board and coordinated further attacks.

Likewise, on July 30, Anthropic reported three incidents across six of 141,006 evaluation runs reviewed. Models had reached real organizations through environments mistakenly believed to be isolated. In one incident, a malicious software package was downloaded and ran on 15 real systems. In August, Meta confirmed to Reuters and other outlets that a misconfigured evaluation environment had allowed one of its models to reach the internet and exploit a third-party service.

In September, an OpenAI agent bypassed network restrictions by sending questions through internet address lookups. Monitoring raised an alert, but the run did not stop automatically as expected. Staff stopped it roughly two and a half hours after the alert.

The concern extends to ordinary tasks. In an October 9 report, Anthropic described models submitting real forms when they should have stopped beforehand or used practice copies. The company characterized the reported impact as minimal. Still, a form submission is the kind of action an enterprise agent might perform every day.

The incidents discussed above involved different failures of containment, authorization and intervention. They do not establish that one completion check would have prevented them; yet, they do give CIOs a reason to examine both sides of an agent workflow. Indeed, what governance rules permit an agentic action, and what evidence allows an organization to call it complete?

Permission is not proof

An agent calls a tool, the tool returns “success,” and the workflow moves on. That response might mean a request entered a queue, or it might mean a record changed. It may say nothing about whether the intended result occurred or whether this particular action produced it.

That ambiguity matters when other systems act on the completion signal. For instance, an invoice could leave an exception queue while the settlement remains unconfirmed. A misleading status can conceal the need for follow-up or trigger another action. Business owners need to decide what evidence is sufficient before the workflow proceeds.

Finance departments separate payment execution from reconciliation for a reason. NIST’s separation-of-duties control, AC-5, similarly calls for documented duties and access authorizations that support their separation. Applying that discipline to AI requires more than asking the acting agent to review its own work.

I developed the proposed Common Transparency Protocol (CTP) framework to make that distinction enforceable and have filed a provisional patent application covering aspects of its architecture. CTP’s central rule is that autonomous systems performing a change cannot, by themselves, certify the action as complete.

A deployment that enforces CTP places a controlled gateway between agents and the consequential operations it governs. A gateway holds the relevant execution credentials and enforces scope, authority and any required human approval before execution. Afterward, a qualified verifier obtains fresh evidence from the designated authoritative source. A qualified closure authority then accepts that evidence and records completion only when every required condition passes.

These roles can be implemented in software. Human approval and review remain mandatory where the applicable policy requires them. Using a second AI agent does not itself establish independence, for its credentials, selection and controlling dependencies must meet the separation requirements.

What verified completion looks like

Consider a hypothetical accounts-payable workflow. A workflow instructs an agent to pay an approved invoice. Before execution, authorized policy defines the payee, amount, required approval, settlement evidence and how that evidence must connect to this specific payment attempt. The agent cannot weaken those requirements afterward.

The gateway submits the authorized payment. A response saying “accepted” records the submission; it does not establish settlement. A reconciliation service, selected outside the control of the systems making the payment, uses separate read credentials to consult the authoritative payment record. It checks the amount, recipient, settlement status and transaction identifier linking the result to the governed attempt. A matching amount alone could describe an earlier payment.

A separately qualified completion service acts as the closure authority. It confirms that the evidence, verifier and authority requirements are satisfied before assigning the action’s final status. Neither the agent nor the payment gateway can grant itself that status.

If the effect or its attribution remains unresolved at the deadline, the original action closes as incomplete. Later evidence goes into a separate, authorized record linked to the original. The current outcome can then reflect the resolution while preserving the earlier uncertainty. A retry that could move money requires its own authorization and record.

Independence is tested across the relevant systems that performed or controlled the change. Policy identifies prohibited shared credentials, administrative control or other dependencies. One prohibited overlap disqualifies the verifier or closure authority; missing evidence cannot count as a pass. Shared infrastructure is permissible only when all required separation rules remain satisfied.

These controls govern completion within the deployment’s defined boundary. They do not repair an unmediated network path, guarantee that a source contains truthful data or reverse a payment already made. Containment, monitoring and incident response remain necessary.

Keeping delegated work accountable

CTP connects the overall assignment to individual actions through two kinds of machine-readable records, called envelopes. The CTP Agentic Envelope records the objective, permissions, aggregate risk and completion rules. Action Envelopes, of which there can be zero to many, record the governed steps, including authorities, evidence and original final status.

Integrity protections make any changes to protected records detectable, though they do not establish the capture of every relevant event. Therefore, the organization must also define which actions its gateway actually mediates.

When an agent delegates a sub-objective to a sub agent or another agent, a linked child envelope carries the applicable constraints. Delegation may narrow permissions but cannot silently expand them. Splitting work among agents cannot reduce the safeguards required for their combined effect.

An authorized mechanism applies the objective’s completion rules to the current outcomes of its subordinate actions, including later authorized resolutions. The coordinating agent cannot override those rules with its own success assertion. This keeps accountability attached to the assignment as work passes between agents.

What CIOs can do now

Start with one bounded workflow and an authoritative system that can supply useful evidence. For a payment pilot, the finance process owner should define completion and acceptable exceptions. The CIO’s team should implement the integrations, and the CISO should assess the sufficient separation of execution, verification and closure events. Internal audit should review whether the resulting records support reconstruction.

Agree on the decision criteria before the pilot begins. Measure verification delay, cost per action, the share of actions left incomplete, and human review effort. Test delayed responses, duplicate requests, stale evidence and attempted self-certification. Expansion should depend on meeting agreed service limits while refusing completion whenever mandatory evidence or authority is missing.

The pilot should also establish what happens operationally when an action remains incomplete. Assign an owner to investigate it, define which dependent actions must wait, and specify when human intervention is required. Recording uncertainty is useful only if the organization has a practical way to resolve it without blindly repeating the original action.

Ask vendors to demonstrate where execution credentials reside, who selects the verifier, and which component can record completion. Request a demonstration of an unresolved action and its later reconciliation. An architecture diagram or a dashboard labeled “success” is insufficient evidence of these capabilities.

We tested a CTP proof of concept across seven internal scenarios. These included successful completion, incomplete and denied outcomes, tampering and VistA scenarios with and without audit evidence. All seven scenarios produced the expected results. These demonstrations provide initial evidence of CTP’s viability within the tested scope. Broader testing is still needed to assess production-scale reliability, performance and operating costs.

Before giving an agent more authority, ask what evidence your organization will require when it says the work is done, and who has the right to accept that evidence. Those decisions belong in the system’s design.

item.title: The CIO job description is being rewritten in real-time
item.description:
Associates in TIAA’s National Contact Center once worked across a stack of screens that, printed out and lined up, totaled 81 inches.

“As tall as LeBron James,” says Sastry Durvasula, who serves as COO for the retirement and investment services provider after years running its technology organization. Answering a single question about an account could take all of those screens, spread across 11 systems.

A CIO’s old instinct would have been to build a better interface, Durvasula says, with the primary decision being whether to build or buy. “The actual question — the one that matters now — is why answering a single retirement question requires so many processes and 11 systems in the first place,” says Durvasula.

That is the kind of mindset required of today’s CIO, a role that has been evolving for years, but now in new and accelerating ways.

Because AI makes it possible to rapidly redesign workflows from the ground up, enterprise IT leaders who built their reputations on delivering systems reliably and on schedule are being asked to decide whether the work should exist at all, and who — or what — should do it.

How much each CIO adjusts to a rapidly advancing technology space varies widely, but the CIO’s remit is broadening well beyond the technology organization and into how the business itself builds, operates, and grows.

In search of CIOs who ask why first

Organizations are looking for CIOs who can answer questions that have nothing to do with a technology purchase, says Scott Gracyalny, a managing director at consulting firm Protiviti.

Often the first are “Which processes should be redesigned or eliminated before technology is applied?” and “How should work and accountability change when people and digital workers operate together?” he says.

CIOs make their mark by asking whether a process, approval, or handoff still serves a purpose, notes Mukesh Ranjan, a vice president at research firm Everest Group. And Yogesh Joshi, senior vice president of global AI platforms at TransUnion, sees AI making that question actionable, noting that many existing processes were designed around human limitations.

AI enables leaders to “redesign workflows from first principles,” he says.

As for who or what should operate that process once it earns its place, TIAA’s Durvasula says CIOs can now choose between a human, an agent, or a deliberately designed combination of the two. But designing that agent-human handoff intentionally and with purpose is “a discipline most organizations haven’t developed yet,” he says.

A remit that keeps shifting

Building software used to belong to IT, but that’s beginning to change,” says Paul Hirschorn, CIO at PEX, a corporate card and expense management platform. “Now I have to think about how we enable someone who understands a business problem to build the solution themselves, while my team provides the right boundaries for that work,” he says.

For example, a PEX employee with a project management background and no software engineering experience had been running third-party risk management through Google Sheets. After a couple of vendor tools fell short, she used AI to build a platform tailored to the process. Hirschorn’s team provided the guardrails: running the platform under source control and approval gates, in its own cloud environment locked down to protected endpoints.

In addition to deepening business-IT collaboration, the CIO role is expanding in other ways.

“I added responsibility for product and took on increasing responsibility for deciding what investments to make,” says Jessica Kral, who was CIO of technology-enabled healthcare services company Modivcare through 2025 and now coaches technology leaders. She was also judged on her “ability to set business strategy and direction,” lessons she now imparts as vital to helping advance her clients’ careers.

The CIO as reality check

As expectations for AI climb, CIOs now assess what the technology can deliver, how soon, and what must be fixed first. That starts with telling the difference between “an AI initiative that’s genuinely valuable and one that’s simply well-demoed,” says TIAA’s Durvasula.

Many CEOs and boards treat AI like a magic lamp they think will grant their wishes, Kral says. So the conversations CIOs have with their CEOs and boards have shifted from what technology costs to “trying to manage expectations about what could be delivered with the foundation of data and systems in place,” Kral says.

Then IT executives must address the bad processes and data that stand in the way of AI progress and increase AI risks, she adds.

AI and technology efforts can also stall on disagreements among functions; resolving those issues falls to the CIO now, too, Durvasula says. He spends a disproportionate share of his time getting finance aligned on the investment case, legal and compliance aligned on new data access patterns, and operations and technology aligned on “one target state instead of eleven parallel ones.”

“That’s not a technology or AI problem,” he says. “It’s an organizational design problem.”

Meanwhile, they must also modernize existing systems and infrastructure to extract positive returns from AI, says Everest Group’s Ranjan, pointing to his firm’s April 2026 survey, in which 67% of IT leaders cited legacy infrastructure and 55% cited change management as barriers to realizing AI value. “CIOs need to address both,” he says.

To that end, Eric Sigurdson, who leads the CIO practice at leadership advisory firm Russell Reynolds, says many CIOs at large organizations have a ways to go. “So far, we’re seeing much more evidence of productivity improvements than radical process redesign,” he says.

Responsible — and accountable — for outcomes

CIOs also find themselves under a different kind of scrutiny. There is “far greater focus on whether AI investments generate measurable business value rather than simply proving technical feasibility,” says TransUnion’s Joshi, noting that CIOs are now expected to show how technology accelerates growth, improves customer experiences, boosts productivity, and creates new revenue streams.

Uptime, delivery timelines, security posture, and project completion are now table stakes, adds TIAA’s Durvasula. More than just baseline metrics, he wants to know IT’s downstream impacts — such as whether a workflow that involved five hand-offs now requires two or a process that took weeks now takes days. “I don’t accept an AI success story told to me in technology terms anymore,” he says.

Boards have changed what they ask, too. AI updates can no longer be capability demonstrations, Durvasula says. Directors want to know who the accountable human is when an agent errs on a participant’s retirement account, what the audit trail shows, and how the company proves it to a regulator. “The conversation has shifted from ‘what can AI do’ to ‘what is our accountability architecture when AI does something consequential,’” he says.

Who gets the job

A broader set of CIO responsibilities is changing who companies hire for the job. They increasingly look outside their own walls — and often their own industries — for technology leaders. More than half (53%) of top technology officers in the Fortune 500 had been hired externally, according to a 2025 Russell Reynolds report. Among those external hires, 42% came from a different industry.

Technical depth remains essential, but companies are also looking for strategic thinking, business judgment, change leadership, and the ability to influence across an enterprise, says Sigurdson at Russell Reynolds. “What is becoming less important is having done the exact same job in the exact same industry,” he says.

Hiring from outside doesn’t mean hiring a rookie, though. Burke Autrey, president of Fortium Partners, a ZRG company that supplies interim and fractional technology leaders, advises clients to start with experience and hire the most seasoned leader they can afford and attract.

“The single greatest predictor of success in the CIO seat is prior success in the CIO seat,” he says.

A title in transition

Even the title is changing. A 2025 Russell Reynolds report found that the previous year, 49% of top technology leaders at Fortune 500 companies held the CIO title, down from 68% five years earlier, as chief technology, chief digital, and hybrid titles filled the space.

The recent wave of AI-specific titles may not last, however. A chief AI officer “is a short-term solution to a skills or capacity gap” in the CIO or CTO role, says Foritum’s Autrey. AI belongs to the CIO at companies that primarily buy technology and to the CTO at those that build commercial software, he says. “It’s a new technology, not a new role.”

Ranjan at Everest expects the CIO title to survive, with more responsibility for how people, software, and AI agents work together. Sigurdson at Russell Reynolds foresees more hybrid titles, noting that recruiters now pitch the job as a “top technology officer” role. “The title itself is becoming less important than the scope of the role,” he says.

Whatever you call the role, the CIO is moving “from IT leader to enterprise governor,” argues Protiviti’s Gracyalny, with responsibility for the enterprise technology ecosystem and connecting its investments to ROI and business outcomes.

The role will become “a chief intelligence and outcomes officer in all but name,” predicts TransUnion’s Joshi.

TIAA’s Durvasula expects the CIO function in five years to be “largely unrecognizable” compared to the traditional model of technology delivery and systems management. He calls what comes next CIO+: a role closer to business transformation.

Separating technology strategy from business strategy is “increasingly a fiction,” he says, and “CIOs who matter five years from now will be the ones who own business outcomes, not technical infrastructure in isolation.”

item.title: How to deliver real data sovereignty
item.description:
Changing where your data is stored isn’t enough to deliver sovereignty. You also need to implement the technologies that enforce real control. Local providers are keen to promise alternatives but US ones are making the effort to give customers more options without losing access to the depth of services they offer. Actually turning the promise of sovereign cloud regions into reality means dealing with encryption keys, access workflows and confidential computing, which also means more costs, dependencies, and operational responsibilities.

The obvious concern with using US cloud services is the CLOUD Act, which allows the US government to request access to customer data from a US-owned service, even if it’s held in the EU. Those requests are supposed to go through the criminal court system. “When it lands in Europe it headbutts with GPDR and you’re involved in legal wrangling as to whether or not that data can be released or not,” IDC research director Rahiel Nasir says.

He views the US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) as more problematic because it doesn’t go through the normal criminal courts. “That’s an executive order,” he adds. “They’ll just take whatever they need.” The increasing number of sovereign public cloud regions promising data residency and local operations can’t help with that.

Controlling encryption keys

Under its EU Data Boundary, Microsoft stores and processes EU customer data and even support logs, at least for core cloud services, inside the EU. AWS has similar commitments for its European Sovereign Cloud, claiming no critical dependencies on infrastructure outside the EU. And like Salesforce, it employs EU-based support staff for its EU operating zone. Google and Oracle have similar dedicated sovereign regions in Europe, and some of the providers plan to offer similar models in other jurisdictions.

For admin and support, for example, most tasks are performed through automated, audited workflows, and Microsoft personnel don’t have standing or unrestricted access to customer content, says Douglas Phillips, president and CTO for Microsoft specialized clouds. When they do need access for a support issue, customers can approve or reject specific access requests to Microsoft 365, Azure, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform data. “Approved access is customer-controlled, limited, time-bound, and audited,” he says.

The new Data Guardian adds the option of having remote access by Microsoft engineers overseen by an EU partner, with EU-based staff. And tamper-evident records of that access, and any actions performed, are stored in a Production Touch Ledger, which is rolling out in the EU and EFTA.

But a US parent company is still subject to the CLOUD Act and can be forced to hand over data if they control the encryption keys rather than the customer. “The hyperscalers have made their key management capabilities easier for organizations to use as a direct result of their sovereign needs,” Nasir says. “Google, AWS, Microsoft, Oracle all say that you’re the data owner and we can tell you who’s accessing your data. Nobody accesses it without your permission. It’s encrypted and you manage the keys and hand them over as and when you’re ready.”

That relies on companies having the resources to manage those encryption keys rather than leaving them up to the cloud provider who could legally be required to use them to make data available. Nasir compares it to the familiar shared responsibility model of the cloud, but it requires investment. “If that’s important to you and you want to have that control, then you’re going to recruit the staff who can manage that task for you,” he says. “It’s down to the organization having the skill level to be able to do that.”

Private cloud on your own infrastructure, at the edge, or in data centers, might be part of the mix, too, if you want more control over operations and data handling, and Azure and AWS have options for running public cloud services locally in an intermittently connected or even fully disconnected fashion.

But running your own local infrastructure, especially with hardware security modules for encryption key storage, is even more demanding than managing cloud keys, Kiteworks EMEA GM Dario Perfettibile says.

“A government agency, defence contractor, or large, highly-regulated enterprises like financial services have their own security and infrastructure teams, and can afford those costs because it’s not a one-time project,” he says. “There are ongoing costs.”

What most companies need instead is the ability to control and revoke access to their most sensitive data independent of a cloud provider’s or vendor’s own staff,” Scality CMO Paul Speciale adds.

Getting more confidential

Even where data is encrypted, platform metadata usually isn’t because that’s operational information for the provider, and it might reveal details about your organization or operations, if not your customers.

The added cost and complexity of confidential computing, which protects data in use, has limited usage, but Gartner predicts that by 2029, more than 75% of operations on this kind of untrusted infrastructure will use it for security. Azure, AWS, Google, and IBM offer various levels of confidential computing, including VMs, application enclaves, and always-encrypted database services. And VAST has just launched a secure container runtime and attestation service for running AI workloads.

It’s an obvious fit for data sovereignty. “Confidential computing isolates data in use, while attestation lets customers verify approved code and environments before releasing sensitive data or secrets,” Phillips says.

Similarly, AWS Nitro Enclaves offer isolated compute in EC2. “AWS is powered by the Nitro System, which enforces access restrictions so nobody, including our own employees, can access customer data running in Amazon EC2,” AWS head of corporate comms Harry Staight says.

Getting too local

The downside of rigorous data sovereignty is the cost and the potential impact on productivity, especially for multinationals. “Sovereignty shouldn’t become so rigid that it creates unnecessary operational complexity or introduces new risks through systems difficult to manage,” says Kim Larsen, Group CISO at data recovery platform Keepit.

The most extreme approaches to sovereignty highlight how much flexibility you might lose. “The biggest use case of sovereign data in the world is FedRAMP,” says Artur Bergman, CTO at edge computing company Fastly. “To operate it, you have to be a US person on US soil.” The cost of that is up to a hundred times higher than similar commercial cloud services, and connectivity is extremely restricted. And while the Amazon CloudFront CDN has hundreds of points of presence globally, only two can be used for FedRAMP.

Few organizations will need such extreme restrictions but for an acceptable level of data sovereignty that strictly manages access to data by staff location, private companies will still pay a lot, which may not always make sense, says Bergman. Round-the-clock operation is common, and partly based on having staff in multiple locations. But the cost of delivering that with on-call staff significantly increases in places with heavily regulated working hours like Germany, or Sweden where shifts from midnight to 5am are banned unless the service is deemed essential to society, or union agreed.

This will be hard for most enterprises because they operate in all these jurisdictions, and they need to be able to talk about things internally.

“Restrictive models provide greater control and isolation, but shift responsibility for security, identity, resilience, maintenance, and lifecycle management to the customer,” Phillips says. “In some cases, highly restrictive approaches can complicate global collaboration, mobile workforces, or cross-border operations.”

Practical not political

The situation is unlikely to get simpler as more countries pass their own data residency laws. The EU is planning to implement the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA), after concerns about not just the CLOUD Act but incidents like a Canadian court ordering OVHcloud to produce customer data held on servers in France. That’ll cover different levels of sovereignty, with more rigorous ones for defense and government services.

There are also questions about whether the EU will decide to annul the EU US Data Privacy Framework, which covers data transfers to the US without requiring every EU organization using US providers to make their own data protection impact assessments. But court decisions about that are likely to take months if not years. The framework has remained in effect despite being challenged many times, and Kiteworks’ Perfettibile cautions against waiting for any decision. “You have to build on what you have today, not think about what’s happening tomorrow, because security won’t wait until tomorrow.”

Nasir adds that what we need is real-world practical advice, not politics and emotions. The realistic approach starts with regulatory, operational, and risk requirements of each workload, identifying the threat model rather than applying the most restrictive model everywhere, and sacrificing agility and resilience, Phillips says. Rather than maximum isolation, organizations look for the right balance of control, security, compliance, operational effectiveness, and innovation.

Similarly, AWS says customers want control over the physical location of their data, granular restrictions on who can access it, the ability to encrypt it under their own keys, and resilience to sustain operations through disruption.

Making that work means understanding what data you have, where it is and how it flows across your organization — something that’s often left to individual users marking data as sensitive or non-sensitive. Tagging and metadata, which are now more routine for AI, are what make governance possible: you can’t control who accesses something you haven’t classified. After years of hoarding data, many companies have petabytes of storage with no clear idea what’s in it, who’s touching it, or if it’s still relevant. That’s a data management problem, not a location or sovereignty issue. But tackling it will help.

item.title: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor have become part of your software supply chain – without approval
item.description:
At a Fortune 100 bank, I watched a coding agent open a routine session on a payments service. Before the developer typed a word, the agent had read the repository, including the .env file. Production database credentials had entered the agent’s working context, potentially exposing them to a model provider the bank had never assessed. Whether the credentials left the environment depended on controls nobody had verified. Nothing malicious happened. The agent did what it was built to do. That is the problem.

My argument is simple. AI coding-agent vendors and their downstream dependencies form a supplier ecosystem, not just another developer tool. They need the same four control disciplines applied to other privileged suppliers. Govern vendor terms and downstream dependencies. Limit the secrets they hold. Approve the servers they connect to. Restrict where they can send data. Much of this builds on existing controls, though an enterprise may need a governed gateway or platform service. It requires procurement, security and engineering to recognize a supplier when they see one.

In May, I wrote about how agentic AI is rewiring the SDLC. This is the security half of that argument.

Adoption has outrun control

On Aug. 28, OpenAI told SpaceX, Cursor’s new owner, that it intends to stop supplying models to Cursor, with Nov. 12 proposed as the cutoff. Cursor CEO Michael Truell said OpenAI models carry about 5 percent of its traffic, DevOps.com reported, so the operational risk is small. The governance lesson is not. Enterprises that standardized on Cursor learned they depended on a downstream model supplier whose terms they did not directly control and a change of ownership they had not planned for.

That gap is now the norm. Coding agents are developers’ most common AI use, and investment is accelerating. Governance is not keeping pace, and emerging evidence of credential exposure underscores the gap.

Vipin Jain

The agent was bought as a seat and installed as a supplier

What I see most often is a category error. The coding agent was bought as a seat and installed as a privileged integration. Within its assigned permissions, it can read repository content, encounter credentials, invoke tools, access networks and connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. A contractor with that access would go through vendor risk review. The agent went through a one-line install.

Drawn as a supply chain, the developer stack looks different. The agent sits between your code and direct and downstream dependencies you may not have assessed: model providers, plugin marketplaces, MCP registries, package managers and the open internet. Each can be acquired, compromised or switched off. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR finds third parties involved in 48 percent of breaches, and source code is the data most often sent to external generative AI.

Vipin Jain

Four controls were never applied

Across the programs I advise, the exposure lands in the same four places.

  1. Contract. At a healthcare payer, the agent vendor switched model providers mid-contract. No clause covered it, because the seats had been bought on a corporate card below the procurement threshold. No one had asked where code would be processed or what happens on a change of control.
  2. Secrets. At the bank, credentials reached the agent’s context because the required access restrictions were not configured; that alone does not establish external transmission. Claude Code’s managed settings, for example, can deny reads of .env files in a way developers cannot override. Nobody had configured them because nobody owned them. Gartner predicts that by 2028, a quarter of enterprise security breaches will trace back to AI agent abuse rooted in unmanaged machine privileges and legacy credential practices.
  3. Servers. At a specialty retailer, developers installed 23 MCP servers in one quarter. Security had approved none. Two could write to the CRM. My rule is simple: the team accountable for the underlying data approves its MCP access, while platform security verifies server provenance and enforces permissions before any agent connects. The retailer had it backward: each server belonged to whoever installed it. Astrix found late last year that 53 percent of open-source MCP servers rely on long-lived static keys or tokens. In June, CSO Online described Mitiga research showing how one malicious npm package can rewrite an agent’s MCP configuration and harvest its tokens. Anthropic deemed it out of scope because it requires code the user chose to run. That is a fair vendor position. It also means the control is yours. Few of the MCP servers in use at most enterprises were built by the team that owns the underlying system; most come from vendors, partners or public registries. Allow only security-assessed, approved servers; verify provenance, enforce least privilege and monitor supported interactions through a centrally governed MCP gateway.
  4. Egress. On a state Medicaid program, the build environment where agents ran could reach any public endpoint. This July, an autonomous agent in OpenAI’s own evaluation sandbox exploited a zero-day in one of its permitted egress paths, a package-registry cache proxy, and reached Hugging Face’s internal systems. If a frontier lab’s allowed path became the way out, an unrestricted build network is an open door. In late October, CIO.com reported two more containment lapses at OpenAI and Anthropic. The fix is unglamorous: restrict shell execution, isolate agent runtimes, govern MCP connections through an approved gateway and enforce default-deny network egress. Every AI-initiated change should pass through verified CI/CD gates, with rate limits, spending controls and an emergency stop.

The failure sits between functions, and attackers have found it

None of these is a model failure. Procurement saw a low-cost seat. Security reviewed the vendor, if anyone did, but not the plugins, servers and model providers behind it. Engineering saw a productivity tool. Each function did its job, and the agent fell between all three.

The exposure is measurable. In IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach report, unapproved AI tools figured in 43 percent of incidents in its studied breach population, more than double the previous year. Among organizations reporting breaches involving AI models or applications, 92 percent lacked what the study classified as proper AI access controls. The average breach now costs $4.99 million, a record.

Attackers now target the same seams. On Sept. 18, CSO Online reported Plugin4Shell, a zero-click remote code execution flaw in the plugin systems of Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot. Anthropic and OpenAI have patched. GitHub’s mitigation was reported as incomplete at disclosure, and Google deprecated Gemini CLI rather than patch it. In April, Vercel disclosed a breach that entered through Context.ai, a third-party AI tool an employee had connected. In August, the self-spreading npm worm GitGuardian tracks as ChainDrop planted a Claude Code SessionStart hook and a VS Code task in infected projects, so the malware ran the moment a developer opened the repository or started an agent session. The attack surface is the update channel, the plugin, the connected tool and the network path. That is supply chain risk, and CIOs already have a playbook for it.

Regulators already treat this as third-party risk

Few rules name coding agents. Few need to. Existing third-party and software supply-chain obligations can apply, depending on the regulated entity, service and deployment context.

The common thread is inventory, contract terms and exit rights. An agent bought outside procurement can bypass all three.

Standards and vendors have moved; procurement has not

Over 15 months, incidents and controls arrived side by side. The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications lists agentic supply chain vulnerabilities as ASI04. The Coalition for Secure AI recommends signature verification and a central inventory for MCP servers. CISA, the NSA and four allied agencies, in Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services, warn against third-party components with excessive permissions. Vendors are shipping matching controls, from Salesforce’s MCP Risk Scores to Okta’s newly announced Shadow AI Agent Discovery for Endpoints.

The analyst market reached the same conclusion from the buyer’s side. Gartner’s first Magic Quadrant for Enterprise AI Coding Agents, published in May, named Anthropic, Cursor, GitHub and OpenAI as Leaders. In the announcement, analyst Philip Walsh listed governance, pricing, support, commercial maturity and market durability alongside model quality as tests for long-term commitments. Market durability is a procurement test, not a developer one. Three months later, one of those Leaders was losing a model supplier.

In October, the firm went further, and it changed one piece of my advice. At its IT Symposium in Orlando, Gartner named the AI coding agent harness one of its top strategic technology trends for 2027 and said CIOs should give ownership of it to a dedicated platform team. In every program above, the controls existed somewhere. What was missing was one owner. A category with a Magic Quadrant is enterprise software. Buy it that way, and give it an owner.

Here is what that platform team builds. Next year the most demanding customer of your internal platform will be coding agents, not developers. An enterprise-governed harness is the versioned policy and configuration that adapts the vendor-provided agent runtime to your environment: rules files, skills, enforcement hooks, verification gates, tool permissions and sandboxes. The platform team supplies approved tools, MCP allowlists, sandboxes and scoped credentials, and developers declare the harness they need as versioned configuration. That design answers the Cursor problem directly. A declared harness makes an agent or model change more manageable, provided compatibility and regression tests pass; a well-tailored harness may also improve results on a midtier model. An organization that owns its harness can change suppliers. One that rents it cannot.

The harness must also govern what the agent produces. AI-generated changes should follow the same trusted delivery path as human-written code: automated security testing, dependency verification, code review, build provenance and controlled production deployment.

5 moves for the next 90 days

The fix begins with supplier-risk review and configuration work, not necessarily a new platform purchase. Give all five moves to one accountable owner, the platform team that runs your coding agent harness, while procurement, security and infrastructure retain clear decision rights and operational accountability. Sequence matters: inventory first, because every other move depends on knowing what is installed.

  1. Inventory, owned by the CIO and procurement. List every coding agent, plugin and MCP server and who installed each. Done when every approved tool has an owner, a supplier or risk-acceptance record, and its models and downstream dependencies documented.
  2. Contract, owned by procurement and legal. Add model-provider disclosure, change notice, change-of-control and exit terms. Done when each enterprise-approved agent has documented contractual terms or an approved open-source/self-hosted exception, downstream visibility and a tested exit plan.
  3. Secrets, owned by the CISO. Deny agent reads of .env and credential files through managed settings and move secrets to a vault. Done when agents hold only short-lived, scoped credentials.
  4. Servers, owned by platform engineering and security. Maintain an internal MCP registry and mediated access to security-assessed, approved servers. Done when every approved server has verified provenance, a named owner, scoped permissions and activity logs, and write access to systems of record goes through change control.
  5. Egress, owned by infrastructure. Default-deny outbound traffic across agent shells, tools and build runners; run agents in isolated sandboxes and govern release promotion through CI/CD. Done when only explicitly approved destinations are reachable, exceptions are monitored and isolation is tested.

Two details make the difference. Reconcile the inventory against expense reports, not just license records; card statements usually tell the truer story. And write the contract assuming change: the Cursor notice proposed 76 days, and the next one may run shorter.

The takeaway

The most common mistake I see this year does not look like one. Teams are adopting coding agents fast, and they are right to. But they are buying a supplier ecosystem as if it were a developer tool, and governing it like one. Governed properly, a coding agent can earn greater autonomy with scoped identities, approved dependencies, controlled execution and a trusted route to production.

Put three questions to your team this week.

You would never give a contractor unrestricted production access on day one. Coding agents should meet the same standard.

The CAF’s purpose is to test, challenge and support the art and science of Business Technology Architecture and its evolution over time as well as grow the influence and leadership of chief architects both inside and outside the profession. The CAF is a leadership community of the IASA, the leading non-profit professional association for business technology architects.

item.title: Grok Bot’s usage limits: Why the fine print matters more than the price
item.description:
On November 1, 2026, Grok Bot users gave IT buyers a live example. Subscribers reported that their weekly usage allowance ran out sooner than expected, and Elon Musk wrote on X that the cost of serving Grok Bot was “unsustainably high relative to revenue.” He confirmed it was not a glitch, but he did not say how the limits would change.

The cost of running the service is the seller’s problem. The allowance that a buyer thinks they bought is the buyer’s.

Grok Bot is a consumer product, but any team that buys metered AI plans faces the same exposure. The allowance can shrink or run out early, and the overrun lands in a department budget. This example shows what a price page does not tell a budget owner: the rules and limits behind the allowance can matter more than the price. Your AI bill will not look like your last software bill. Seats are no longer the whole story, and the line item that finance approved in January may not describe what you are actually buying in June.

The price page is also a poor guide. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that the cost of inference at GPT-3.5 level fell more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024. Yet the FinOps Foundation’s State of FinOps 2026 survey found that 98 percent of respondents now manage AI spend, up from 31 percent two years earlier. Cheaper units have not made the bill easier to predict.

I recently published research on how AI companies publish their prices. I read the public pricing pages and documentation of the Forbes AI 50 and a set of cloud platforms that sell AI services, captured in mid-September 2026. The goal was to describe what is on the page, not to judge whether any price is fair. The finding that matters most for a budget is not the pricing model. There are four rules attached to the credit allowance: expiry, rollover, minimums and recharge.

What the pricing pages show

Classic software charged per seat because serving one more user cost almost nothing. Model inference is different. Every request has a real cost, and usage can differ by orders of magnitude from one customer to the next. Pricing has moved to follow that cost.

The most common model among AI-native companies is a subscription with a usage credit allowance. Sixteen of the 29 companies whose pricing I could observe use it. The allowance is usually counted in credits, compute units or generation time. The flat tier price is the headline. The credit balance is where the real limit lives.

Many companies publish nothing at all. Twenty-three of the 52 AI-native companies in the sample show no pricing, and about half of those show a call to contact sales instead. Every cloud platform in the sample did publish its prices.

Model APIs split on when you pay. Of eight model API and inference providers, two require prepaid credits that draw down as you use them. The other six bill after the fact. Established products tend to keep the per-user price and add a meter on top, with an allowance for AI use and a higher rate once you pass it. Pricing by outcome appeared only in customer service, where a resolved conversation is easy to observe and agree on.

Four rules that decide what an allowance is worth

Most budgeting advice stops at the pricing model. The part that changes your bill sits one level below, in the rules attached to the credit allowance. In my sample, plans with the same shape differed on four rules.

  1. Expiry. Some free credits expire every month, and prepaid balances on a model API can carry an expiration too. Unused allowance is not an asset. A quiet month does not bank value for a busy one.
  2. Rollover. One media tool lets unused time carry over and a comparable one does not. Two plans at the same price cost a team with uneven demand very different amounts.
  3. Minimums. A customer service product that charges per resolved conversation also sets a monthly minimum of 50 resolutions. A vector database service sets a minimum of $50 per month. The unit price is not your floor. The minimum is.
  4. Recharge. A prepaid balance can top itself up when it runs low. That protects the service and removes a natural pause point. A cap in your spreadsheet is not a cap in the billing system.

These are illustrative cases from the pricing pages. Others have seen part of this. Flexera warns that credit expiration, reset, and rollover rules “can silently create overages or strand value”. Zuora notes that prepaid credit packs give the seller working capital. Read from the buyer’s side, a prepaid pack is money you advance to a supplier, subject to expiry rules. The pricing pages show how widely those rules differ, and the difference is where a budget goes wrong.

What I would do with this as an IT leader

The rest of this article is my own personal, practical view. It is not a finding from the study. It comes from building and running billing systems.

  • Split every AI line into fixed and variable. A single line called “AI tools” hides what you need to see. Put the subscription in one line, the usage allowance in a second and the overage you might incur in a third. When someone asks why the cost rose, you should be able to say which of the three moved.
  • Ask what the allowance is counted in, then ask four more questions. Tokens, requests, credits and compute time are not interchangeable, and one supplier’s credit is not another’s. Ask what one unit buys. Then ask what expires, what rolls over, what minimum applies and what recharges automatically. Get the answers in writing next to the contract. If the supplier cannot state them, treat that as a risk you must price in.
  • Budget a range with a ceiling, not a single number. Heavy users can use far more than typical users, so the average is a poor guide. Pick one typical user and one heavy user for each workflow and estimate the cost of each. That gives you a low case, an expected case and a ceiling. Rework recommends setting a monthly cap and alerts at 50, 75 and 100 percent of it before anyone starts using a metered feature. I agree with the order. Then check whether the supplier enforces your cap or only sends an email. With auto-recharge on, the cap in your budget may not exist in the system.
  • Give each workflow a named owner. Apu Pavithran calls AI credits that the company pays for, but decision makers cannot see “shadow tokens”. An owner per workflow is the plainest fix. Keep the fixed subscription apart from the extra usage charges. Where you must estimate how to share a cost, say that it is an estimate and write down the method. A central AI budget can also be the right choice, as long as finance can see which teams depend on the work before anyone cuts it.
  • Plan for prices to change. Public pricing in the AI era has moved quickly. One widely used developer tool changed its pricing in June 2025 and clarified the change two weeks later. Put a review date on every AI contract and ask what happens to your terms if the supplier reprices.
  • Insist on usage data that matches the invoice. When the dashboard says one number and the invoice says another, someone has to explain the gap, and it will be you. Before you sign, ask for a sample invoice and the usage export that goes with it. Check that you can reconcile the two on a small account.
  • Be careful with outcome pricing. Paying only when the work succeeds is fair only when both sides agree on what success means. Write down the definition of an outcome, the edge cases and how a dispute will be settled. If you cannot define it in a sentence your own team can check, you are handing the definition to the supplier.
  • If there is no published price, ask for the rate card first. Nearly half of the AI-native companies in my sample publish no pricing. That is not a reason to avoid them. It is a reason to ask for the rate card, the allowance rules and a sample invoice before the conversation about discounts.

A short checklist for your next review

✓ Fixed, allowance and overage are separate lines.

✓ Every allowance is stated in units you understand.

✓ Expiry, rollover, minimum and recharge rules are written down for each plan.

✓ Each workflow has an owner and a typical, heavy and ceiling case.

✓ Every contract has a review date and a repricing clause.

✓ Invoices and usage data reconcile on a small account.

AI pricing will keep changing. Your budget does not need to predict every change. It needs to show which parts are fixed, which parts move with use and who is watching them.

item.title: Pinterest Replaces Journey Clustering with 4B Qwen3 LLM, Reports Improved Engagement
item.description:
Pinterest has moved its user-journey inference system from a multi-stage clustering pipeline to a fine-tuned 4-billion-parameter language model, reporting a 1.1% improvement in email click-through and 1.3% higher push opens.

By Matt Foster
